Zei started planting one last major structure by hand: a symbol-carrying spaceship. There were already four created by his AI, but he figured that he would make one all on his own, so that Bai would not see it, and with a different style of moving wall in front of it. He aimed the symbol-carrying spaceship so that it would reflect off a wall that his AI had already constructed, and then move upwards along the middle of the game field.

"PA GU..."

Come on, Zei thought, finish the symbol-carrying spaceship.

"SO ... BI ... ZE ... HA ..."

Zei put down a few last squares.

"MU ... FO ..."

And... done.

Zei let out a long breath.

"SHI ... LE ... PA ... TAU FA"

Gliders started flying. Zei's symbol-carrying spaceship started moving west from the southeast corner. The portion of the game field that Zei could see increased.

Both AI transcripts were focused intensely on exploiting their territories, building more gliders, spaceships and walls, and expanding.

After a few hundred turns, Zei and Bai's gliders began to crash into each other, and then into each other's spaceships and walls.

And a few hundred turns after that, their symbol-carrying spaceships got within sight of each other.

Shortly after that, Zei's symbol-carrying spaceship reflected off the wall in the south, and began moving north.

On the big screen, the audience watched.



The first intervention turn came. Zei let his AI do the work adjusting structures near the frontline, as the consequences would be immediately visible to Bai anyway.

He scanned Bai's AI's transcript for weak points. He found one: it was not thinking at all about glider attacks coming down the diagonals. He toned down the amount of resources allocated to the AI, and used those resources to manually send a large number of gliders down both diagonals, targeted so that one would pass right after the other, to strike both of Bai's home bases. He also sent a symbol-carrying spaceship, targeted to pass the center hundreds of turns after both sets of gliders.

The game continued.

The battle along the front lines in the middle was surprisingly even-handed. Both AIs were playing near-optimally, and there was little opportunity for trickery because both sides could see each other's moves and thoughts. However, Bai did put more resources toward the frontline especially on the west side, and as the hundreds of turns went on, it began to show on the board. Soon, one of Zei's symbol-carrying spaceships on the west was breached, and it exploded into a storm of gliders flying in all directions.

Zei kept playing, optimizing the minutiae of the game board. He knew that he would not get to see the results of his attack for a long time.

The second intervention turn came.

The best that Zei could come up with was constructing more factories beside his symbol-carrying spaceship that was slowly flying north along the middle of the field. Aside from the attack down the diagonal, this was the one structure that Bai had no way of knowing about - unless his AI decided to ignore Zei's instruction to focus exclusively on the domain it was assigned to, and blurted out the spaceship's position mid-transcript. Zei decided to ignore that possibility; not much he could do about it anyway. He put up more walls along the west side.

More turns passed. On the west side, Bai continued to advance. Some of Bai's gliders got into Zei's base in the southwest, and destroyed two of his symbols. Zei watched as his symbol-carrying spaceship made its way toward the northwest.

Then, suddenly, gliders flew at the spaceship from the west, north and east side. It quickly crumbled, and exploded into rubble and a dozen gliders. At that point, Zei realized what had happened. Bai's AI's lack of thought about the diagonals had not been a mistake at all. Rather, Bai had deliberately directed the AI to focus on the other directions, and she had put up a strong multilayered defense along the diagonals herself. It had been a trap, and Zei had fallen squarely into it.



Mu felt a pang of disappointment in Zei. Seventeen symbols to twenty-two, she thought. How could he have fallen into that trap, and not come up with anything interesting himself? He had one spaceship going north in the middle, but so what? Bai's bases were well protected against attacks along the diagonals, and Zei's spaceship did not have excellent chances of reaching the north side. Unless Zei came up with something totally unexpected, she figured, this would turn into a game of attrition, which would only shift further in Bai's favor.

An unexpected set of gliders knocked out another two of Zei's symbols, one slightly southwest of the center of the field, and another slightly west of the center near the south end. Another set of gliders unexpectedly hit Zei's southeast base, but bounced off harmlessly against now well-prepared walls.

Sitting on the other side of the room, in less comfortable public seating, Fin gazed with fear at the gameboard as well.

Finally, something inside of Zei's mind clicked.

"Take my fourth westernmost symbol", he told the AI. "Take the best sixteen strategies that you can come up with. Construct near that symbol a factory capable of executing each of those strategies. It should be activated by a glider coming in from the southwest, and the exact strategy chosen should depend on the type of glider and the time it hits. Then, near my second westernmost symbol, make that glider. Allocate eighty percent of resources this intervention turn to this."

The AI started thinking in detail, implementing the factory, and the glider.

Bai's AI started thinking about countermeasures to all sixteen strategies, but soon hit a limit: it could not optimize defenses against all of them at the same time.

Bai's AI also focused on increasing defenses across her own western flank. Zei's first gamble paid off, he realized: Bai herself did not realize just how much damage she had done on the west side, and just how little Zei had done to compensate. And so neither she nor her AI realized that by this point, Zei's fourth westernmost symbol could be in the middle of the field.

Then, Zei went to work on his second gamble. He used the resources he had not allocated to the AI to add a brick south of his factory to block the glider that the AI was sending, and add two of his own gliders coming in from the south.

The intervention turn ended. Part of the factory had been built during the intervention turn, the rest continued to be constructed in real time out of nearby rock formations by gliders.

A few hundred turns later, the glider sent by Zei's AI from the west was blocked by the brick that Zei had put in place. A few hundred turns after that, the gliders that Zei sent manually crashed into the factory, and activated it.

The factory picked a strategy that was none of the four that Bai's AI had focused on planning for. And it was coming from a place that Bai had not expected: the halfway point between the center of the board and the northern edge. The factory quickly started generating symbol-carrying spaceships that began to move toward the east, and a storm of gliders that moved north, and then bounced off of rock formations and Bai's own walls to move toward the west. Bai, and her AI, were caught completely by surprise.

By the time the next intervention turn came, Zei's spaceships had gotten well behind Bai's lines on the east. Zei's AI took the opportunity to design a storm of gliders to attack Bai's flanks from behind, and Zei added a few of his own gliders to attack Bai's northeastern base - building them himself so that they would not appear in the transcript.

Five hundred turns after that, the game board looked very different.



By this point, Mu's solemn head shaking and Fin's expression of fear had both turned into excited smiles.

Fourteen to eleven. Zei was winning again. And he had a better position.

Soon, the next intervention turn came. At this point, Zei figured, he would just repeat the same strategy, though a more near-term version of it: immediately create many glider factories in the northeast, and have their exact style and direction be set off by a trigger that would only appear in ten turns. Bai could not see the exact internal logic of the trigger, and Zei designed that piece himself, so that it would not appear in the transcript.

Bai attempted to copy Zei's strategy. Zei spent half his resources generically shoring up his defenses, without attempting to be particularly clever in outsmarting Bai. He was reasonably safe, he knew: Bai simply did not have any positions behind his lines the way he had behind Bai's.

Five hundred turns later, both attacks came to fruition. Zei's succeeded, Bai's failed. Bai's only significant accomplishment was destroying the remaining symbols in Zei's southwestern base.



Twelve to six.

Bai resigned.

The audience cheered.

"Congratulations, you two-", Mu began to speak, standing in the waiting room along with Zei and Bai.

"Congratulations, Zei. You only had to wait until our last season to beat me."

"You played the best game of your life today, Bai."

Mu paused for a few moments.

"The priests did not even know what you two would come up with. They told me that they wanted to make the game a little more ... realistic - but they were as curious as anyone else to find out what that means."

"Realistic?", Bai exclaimed incredulously. "How is it at all realistic that AIs can read each other's minds?"

"It sounded crazy to me too. But the more I think about it, the more I've come to see their point."

"Look at the Veridian Steering system, for example. It's one of the most opaque parts of the government - even the Keepers don't know who each other are - and yet one of the most trustworthy and incorruptible parts precisely for that reason. Similar for the Courts - anonymous, randomly selected committees out of a large pool."

"But the Parliament is transparent, and so when it comes to the Parliament's direct decisions - large-scale infrastructure, foreign policy, healthcare, all the things that it's funding - everyone keeps exploiting and outsmarting it. Same with the quadratic funding - actually, it's even worse. Keepers, Sentinels and Court judges are not fully insulated - it is still Parliament committees that are approving them - but at least there's a layer of indirection there, and those positions are also gated by prediction scores."

"That's the lesson. In the real world, it's not just thinking well that matters, it's also hiding your thoughts - sometimes, even hiding your thoughts from your allies or the people you're meant to serve."

Zei and Bai both stared at Mu.

"Anyway, you've both performed extremely well today."

A robot slid in carrying two bags, one with the number 1 on the side and the other with the number 2.

Mu handed the first bag to Zei and the second bag to Bai.

Zei and Bai both sat down and started looking at the contents inside their bags. A plaque, a scratch-off one-time-scannable code containing some cryptographic tokens and credentials, and smaller gifts: a cup, a handwriting instrument, and an ozone-based electric water disinfection pen.

Bai began studying all of the gift items in detail. Zei immediately started to scratch off the cover from the scannable code, and took out his hand device to prepare to scan it. He had been hoping to be able to buy his mom a new compute box for many months now, and he still could not believe that now he could finally actually get it.

Mu stood up.

"I hope you both have a good rest", she said, as she turned and began to leave the room.

As soon as Mu was gone, Zei noticed that he got one gift that Bai did not: a dark purple letter, with an inscription on the front.

dun fe tin di zei de kin kie

"For Zei's eyes only"

Zei stopped scratching the cover on the scannable code, and instead put the letter into his pocket.

Out of the corner of his eye, he saw more people than usual looking intently at their hand devices at that moment. Curious, he stepped forward and quietly looked at what one of the other passengers was looking at.

"Veridia National University", the header at the top of the view on the passenger's hand device said. "Live debate between Professor Sylka, president of VNU, and Lord Ephelion, Arctic ambassador to Veridia".

Sylka was speaking, and Gladias could make out the subtitles.

"Gross economic output alone measures one part of human progress", she said - though Gladias could only see and not hear. "But it becomes a very limiting and impoverished perspective if you start viewing it as the entire goal."

Gladias was curious enough that he whispered to Emerald through his neck band to put up an audio livestream of the debate.

"There is so much more that matters. There is the citizens' health, their emotional well-being, and how healthy the bonds in the society are."

As Sylka finished speaking, the audio livestream connected. Gladias stepped back from the passenger, somewhat embarrassed that he had momentarily violated the passenger's privacy by looking at his screen, and relieved that he was now receiving the feed in a completely ethical way.

"What good is a large car if people feel unhappy because they have no purpose in life? What good is a large house if people feel alienated in their society, and don't have friends to invite to it?"

"What good are the latest electronics, if the people at the bottom use them to hack and steal, the people at the top use them to invade people's privacy and surveil, and everyone all the time uses them to get outraged on social media platforms?"

"Such questions are the entire reason why Veridia has mechanisms like Steering."

Sylka paused. Lord Ephelion started speaking.

"There has now been a century-long tradition of people trying to make better metrics than gross economic output. But what we have seen is that especially over the long term, the countries that perform best on any of those metrics are precisely the ones whose economic output is highest."

"And there is a deep reason for this. Historians have long understood that many phenomena in society move in cycles. The ancients talked about a cycle: flourishing, pride, arrogance, downfall, suffering, rebirth, and then flourishing once again. They said the same thing about governance, and how it inevitably cycles between technocratic, democratic, chaotic and strongman."

"Whenever we talk about the inevitability of rises and falls, it is precisely these 'softer' traits like 'societal cohesion', 'freedom' and 'well-being' that move in this fashion. On those dimensions, the dominant transformation is a rotation: good creates the generator of the bad, which creates the bad, which creates the generator of the good once more."

"And let us be real: these 'softer' traits that people are targeting, they're chosen by committees of priests - selected not for competence, but for echoing whatever ideology strikes people's fancy at the time."

"There is only one thing that stands out from this pattern and offers a truly lasting improvement: the relentless march of economic growth, enabled by the unceasing progress of science, technology, and capital accumulation. While the emotional vibrations in a society cycle between the pride of success, and the desperation of collapse and defeat, with every cycle, people are smarter and richer than before."

Gladias could see the eyes of a few of the people on the autobus watching perking up.

"The Order members are chosen by a sophisticated-"

"Order, please. Ephelion has the floor.", the moderator interjected.

"And so if you want to truly improve a society, in a way that provides lasting value for the long term, you do not focus on the thing that moves in cycles. You do not focus on accelerating the rotation. Instead, you focus on increasing the largest eigenvector. You focus on affecting the thing that has a thousand-year record of compounding on itself, the vector on which good reliably leads to more good. And you let the rest follow the natural laws as it may."

Ephelion stopped, and Sylka cleared her throat, preparing to speak. At that point, Gladias realized that the autobus door was open, and it was already at his destination. He quickly ran out, and Emerald automatically paused the livestream to help him concentrate.

She went quiet, and sat back in her chair. She had not planned to say any of that. After a brief pause, she spoke again.

"But those tactics of Zei's, they were beautiful. I was so proud when I put up such perfect defenses along my diagonals and tricked Zei into attacking there. I felt like that was the smartest thing I had done in my whole life. And then he came out and did something even smarter."

"I do want to understand you guys better. What drives you, how you think."

Bai and Fin both took a brief break to drink some of their respective teas.

"Let's talk about something else. Here, do you want to see what they have in mind for the next version of Dzegoban?"

Bai's eyes perked up.

"Sure, why not", she replied.

Fin took out his booklet, with "po so dze go ban de sia" - the conception of Dzegoban version nine - on the cover.

"Dzegoban is a masterpiece", Fin explained. "Always navigating the tough balance between being easy to learn, logical in syntax, but also nice to speak and read, and useful for talking about the things that people care about in the real world."

"The first versions, started only a decade after we lost the war against the Arctics last century, were simple and uncontroversial. Move from the pictorial script to an alphabet, get rid of the complicated declensions and conjugations and irregular verbs."

By this point, Bai was listening intently, her eyes full of curiosity.

"Then came the harder tradeoffs, on the grammar. Dzegoban grammar is very logical, if you want it to be. Take a simple sentence, like in elementary school: 'giu jan li mo fe jia dzu lie'. The man eats the avocado. 'li' is the separator between subject and verb, 'fe' is the separator between verb and object. A computer program can parse that, very unambiguous."

"You can get more complex. 'lo mo fe jia dzu lie zo hen jun'. It's healthy to eat an avocado. 'lo' and 'zo' are the opening and closing brackets. And colloquially, you can leave out the 'lo'."

"But then you get ambiguity. Let's unpack 'jia dzu lie' - black center fruit. Is it a fruit with a black center, or is it a fruit that is both black and 'central' in some sense? Theoretically, we have the separator for that: 'ji'. We could say 'jia dzu ji lie', and it would be less ambiguous. But you can never remove the ambiguity completely. Papaya seeds have a black center too."

"So you have to balance regularity with practicality. Being easy and pleasant to speak when you talk about things that are common in people's lives. So the Bansunpei priests tried to optimize the regularity of the meaning space, even while knowing they would never - could never - fully succeed."

"If all you know are the 256 roots, you can understand more than half of what people are saying. Not all, but much better than the olden days, when you could not tell what some complicated word means at all unless you had seen that exact word before."

"Why are they putting so much work into this? Why not focus more on improving the economy, or technology, or the military or something?"

"Well, if we work on those things, the Arctics bomb us. Language is harmless. I think even the Arctics find Dzegoban impressive. Also a couple of times the Bansunpei took time to reform the timing system - that's how we got a hundred ticks a minute, a hundred minutes a longhour and ten longhours a day - and we got that to stick across the whole world. That, even the Arctics adopted."

"Do you guys have a secret textbook with a planned version nine of that?"

"Yeah, at some point we want to replace the meter with the lightfoot. Light travels at one billion lightfeet per tick. One lightfoot is two hundred fifty-nine point oh two oh six eight three seven one two millimeters."

"Apparently, people in Inglewore like it because for so long people made fun of their older measurement units for being complicated and illogical, and now we're coming out with a unit that's very close to their older distance unit in length, that's directly based on the very base physical constants of the universe. So in some sense, we're saying that they were right all along."

Bai grinned.

"So anyway, the next version of Dzegoban-"

Bai cut him off.

"Maybe next time. This is all making me curious, I feel like I should go study the history of Dzegoban on my own at some point."

"Good instinct! I promise, it gets even more fun once we get into version nine. Zei doesn't see the value of all this himself, he's so focused lately on his games."

"I'm sure he is. And I don't think it will stop, it's clearly paid off very well for him."

"Maybe I should play some games with him for fun - or I guess for him, for practice - at some point."

"Oh, and thank you for distracting me and cheering me up!"

Zei walked through the tunnel, and down the stairs, following the directions that his watch gave him. Every time he got to a fork, he made sure to look in all directions, taking in his surroundings. He had never been this deep into the depths of the mountain pyramid before.

Eventually, he got to a sealed door with a green circle beside it. He tapped his watch against the circle. The door slowly opened.

Behind the door, there was a narrow and long room, and at the end of the room there was a large table. At the table, a man was sitting wearing a shadowy cloak - not a Veridian privacy robe, but the dress of the Minpentai priests.

Zei walked across the room slowly, and sat down across from the priest.

"Welcome", the priest said softly.

"I am honored to be here", Zei replied. "But ... who are you?"

"I'm Den. High Council member of the Kungaupei. Thank you for coming."

"Kungaupei? We have a secret society for defense too? Growing Dzego a whole secondary shadow army?"

"Of course, are you surprised?"

Zei hesitated.

"I was impressed by your performance in the Minpentai game a few days ago."

"But I wasn't just impressed because you won. I studied the transcripts from the game. I was impressed because of the kind of strategy that you played."

"Tell me, have you studied any cryptography?"

"I... know the basics? Factoring is hard, you cube modulo n to encrypt, and only someone who knows the p times q that make up n can invert the cubing to decrypt."

"No no, that's popular science cryptography. Nobody has been using the factoring-based stuff for decades now, even elliptic curves are falling out of fashion because everyone's worried that the Arctics are going to come out with a quantum computer any year now."

Zei did not respond. He stared back, in a mix of appreciation for the update to his knowledge, and curiosity about where this whole conversation was going to lead.

"Okay, well I think in your last game you've come really close to inventing big parts of cryptography from scratch."

"Think about obfuscation protocols. You want to give someone a program, that they can execute, without being able to see the internal details of the program. It's what our modern cryptographic networks - like the ones that handle payments and reputation and manage governance for Dzego's secret societies - all rely on."

"But how do you make a single protocol that can do that? Hide the program? It's easy to see how to hide the data, and then do addition and multiplication on hidden data, especially when it's all done by hiding it in big vectors under linear transformations and adding errors on top. But how do you hide a program? What kind of a space of possible programs do you even hide a program in?"

"The solution - well, okay, a small part of one type of solution - is that you create a meta-program. A program that, depending on its input, can run any possible program. And then you've reduced the program to just being a set of numbers that you're doing addition and multiplication to."

"It's one of the most basic tricks in computer science. Our computers, the physical hardware, are meta-programs themselves. But you figured out a really basic version of that - just sixteen possible algorithms, melded into one factory - and used that, plus a hidden glider to provide the input, to hide your intentions."

Zei nodded.

"Well thank you for the compliment. But ... I'm curious now, where are you going with this?"

"Well, Zei, I want to recruit you into defense."

Zei's eyes and mouth opened.

Defense. Without thinking, Zei opened and closed each finger of his left arm. That arm had been broken and taken a month to heal, all because of a thermodynamics lecture. What Den was suggesting was not a lecture.

But his life had been saved by exactly that kind of work - a secretive, well-coordinated room change at the last minute. Maybe this was his chance to do the same for someone else.

"I do want you to continue Minpentai into the nationals. I think it will be good for you. But for your education, do cryptography. I think it will also help you in your games."

"And of course I'll stay in touch the whole way, and when you're ready, I will start suggesting some tasks for you."

Zei responded with silence once again.

Tasks. He noticed how quickly Den had shifted into the register of assuming that Zei would go along with his plans. Part of him was already coming up with reasons to say yes. Another part was watching his enthusiasm slowly build up, and did not entirely trust it.

"I have an idea", Den began. "Do you know how chip verification works? Like, how I'm automatically verifying that all your electronic devices are friendly right now?"

Zei began to reply as soon as Den finished. By sheer luck, Den had decided to grill him on one of the areas of applied cryptography that he had already researched.

"When a device is manufactured, a physical unclonable function is produced as part of the process - a secret key that gets generated though chemicals settling down as the chip cools down after it's produced. Not even the manufacturer knows what it is. The manufacturer prods the device to get its public key - the p times q, or I guess now I know it's not a p times q at all, it's something totally different. It then signs that key with its key, and publishes that to the cryptographic network."

"Okay I guess you can call a function a key, close enough. Go on."

"As a user, you can ask the device to sign a value. The device will do that. You can then verify its signature against the public key that you download from the cryptographic network, to check that it actually came from that manufacturer."

"And then you have public inspectors. They buy devices randomly from the manufacturer, and use some kind of scanning to destructively inspect them. Verify that the chips actually have the logic that they are supposed to have."

"Why the cryptographic network? Why not just sign it?"

"So that you know how many there are, avoiding attacks where either the manufacturer is cheating or someone hacks their key, and they start signing over even more public keys than they should. Also it means you know when the signature was made, so you know it was made when the device was manufactured. And if the manufacturer's key somehow gets stolen, you can tell if the signature was made before or after that happened."

"And how do I verify your device?"

"You ask it for a signature wirelessly, same way I verify it."

"How do I know it's not just forwarding responses from a different device somewhere else?"

"Here, because we're deep inside a mountain. Generally, I don't know."

"How does the chip inspection process work?"

"That I don't know."

"How do the inspectors know that they're getting devices from the same pool the public is getting, and not devices specifically chosen by the manufacturer to fool them?"

"I don't know."

"Let's think about a different case first. Take the public security cameras, the ones on the lamp posts or the outsides of the buildings or the autobuses. Every Dzegojan has a right to occasionally randomly pick one, unscrew it and analyze it themselves. That's how we know that they're only recording and transmitting when they're supposed to, and no one in the supply chain from the people manufacturing them right up to the people installing them can bug them and leak any data to a stalker or an insider trader or an Arctic."

"That's the random inspection process - assuming at least some of the people who make inspecting cameras their hobby actually choose randomly. So that's for security cameras, that are already in public so anyone can just choose a random one of them to go and unscrew. Now, what do we do here? How do we do random inspection for computer chips that you buy from a manufacturer?"

"Okay, you tell me."

"Well, I'm glad there's still a lot that I can teach you. How about we go and visit one of these factories right now?"

Zei thought for a moment. It was not yet a commitment, he reasoned, and it would be something he had never seen before.

"Sure, would be happy to!"

Zei and Den walked out of the room, through the tunnels, and to a smaller exit from the pyramid. The exit led directly into the interior of a large rectangular-shaped black car. The pyramid door and the car door were exactly the same shape, and were pressed tightly against each other.

Zei and Den got in.

As the door sealed shut, Zei noticed anti-transmission foil lining the sides of the car. The car had windows, but they seemed to show a dimmed version of the world outside; from the outside, he knew, they would show almost nothing at all.

The car started moving, and a minute later it entered a tunnel.

At that point Zei realized that no one in the world now knew where he was.

Zei and Den got out of the black car. The car's door now opened directly into the open door of a staircase leading down to a basement, shielding them from even a tick of being visible to the outside. The two walked down the stairs, and eventually entered a large room.

They saw thousands of empty white boxes, with labels on the side containing a two-dimensional barcode, and a machine automatically putting chips into boxes as they came out of a conveyor belt from another room.

Den opened up his hand device, and showed a diagram to Zei.



"You ever seen this before?", Den asked.

"Some kind of diagram of the internet?"

"It's a mixnet. It's how transactions get onto the cryptographic network without people being able to see who sent them."

"Each message from each sender gets wrapped with three layers of encryption. That top-level message gets sent to a node on the first layer."

"The node on the first layer unwraps the top layer of encryption, and sees another encrypted message, along with the address of which node in the second layer they are supposed to send it to."

"The node on the second layer unwraps the next layer of encryption, and sees another encrypted message, along with the address of which node in the third layer they are supposed to send it to."

"Finally each node on the third layer unwraps that layer of encryption, and gets the address of the destination, plus the actual payload. And of course, usually, the payload itself is encrypted."

"Wow, I didn't realize that's how it works. So you need three nodes to collude to unmask the sender of a message."

"Not just three nodes - three randomly selected nodes. And if you're paranoid, you can make the inner payload be yet another envelope, requesting to send the message right back through the system in the next round."

"So this is what the packaging step is doing. Those boxes are highly opaque and tamper-proof sealed, and the two-dimensional barcode is the encrypted payload. It's a mixnet, but for delivery of physical goods."

"If you buy a product through this system, only the last of the three nodes knows your address, and they don't know who the sender was or what they're delivering. And if you're double paranoid, you can set your address to a public drop-off point and pick it up yourself."

"Inspectors buy through the mixnet. And so as a consumer, if you buy through the mixnet yourself, you're getting your chip from the same pool that the inspectors are buying from - the manufacturer has no way to give an honest chip that passes inspection to the inspectors, without almost certainly giving one to you too. They can't tell which chips - or whatever other physical goods are passing through this thing - are going to whom."

Den then walked forward toward a door. Zei followed him.

Den put his watch against a circle with a glowing green outline. The door opened.

They walked through a hallway, took a few turns, and then went through another door. They entered a room with a large microscope.

"This is the inspection facility of this fab. They inspect both their own chips, and those produced by others."

"They do multiple types of three-dimensional scanning, at different wavelengths, to make sure that the physical chip exactly matches the specification."

"I'm impressed. Say thank you to whoever gave you permission to give us a tour."

"I will. So Zei, I remember you had another question."

"Yeah I remember. Though it wasn't about manufacturing."

"Indeed - it was about how someone verifying could know that responses are not being forwarded from a different device. I can tell you the answer for that too. My hand device has a protocol by which it repeatedly contacts each device a million times, and expects the whole protocol to finish within a tenth of a tick. And so wherever the signature comes from, it has to be within fifty lightfeet away - almost thirteen meters - actually, even closer, because of the latency of the chips themselves."

"So Zei, what do you think?"

"You said I can still do the nationals, right?"

"I want you to do the nationals."

"Okay yes, I'll join - or at least, I'll commit as far as switching my studies to cryptography and see how that goes."

Den nodded.

When Den kept walking forward, Zei's mind wandered - first, to the large microscope that was directly in front of him, and then to other matters.

He started thinking about what he would tell his mom that afternoon. He could talk about Fin being busy, about himself going for a walk. But he could not tell the full truth. The Kungaupei forbade it - and his mom had already watched him heal from one bomb.

Chapter 10

Freetown, United Cities·3724 Windmoon 24

Jahn's taxi pulled up at the Freetown Economics Institute, where he worked as a researcher, and he got out of the car. He entered the building, and tapped his hand device to pay to get through the turnstile.

Out of the corner of his eye, he noticed that the entrance price was ten percent higher than before.

He walked to the restaurant section, and saw most tables full. Only one table had empty space, and there was already a woman sitting there.

"Can I sit down here?", Jahn asked.

"Of course."

Jahn sat down.

"I'm Jahn", he offered.

"I'm Utaku. I'm from Belpaki, I'm doing my doctorate program here at the Institute."

A robot slid up to Jahn, offering a menu.

Jahn quickly scanned through, and ordered a dish with vegetables and fish, and a glass of water.

He noticed that there too, the prices were higher than before.

"Wow, the prices are all up now."

"Haven't you been following the news?"

"Not since I got back from a meeting in Hapton."

"Huh, well it should be news in Hapton too. Everyone's been talking about raising their defense budgets."

"Arctic scare?"

"Yeah, their drone activity has been going up. Though there's surprisingly many politicians who seem totally nonchalant about it. Only Redshire and its neighbors seem to be really taking it seriously."

"Well, somehow, also Freetown."

"Why us? I'm glad we are, but like half the United Cities are closer to Redshire than we are, they should be worrying more!"

"Well, Devanvil is taking it seriously - after all, Redshire chooses twelve percent of the seats in Devanvil's parliament. But yeah, Deplexi, Ondak, Imber, not at all."

"It is weird. Remember, the government here is constitutionally banned from collecting more than the basic land tax and some rent from its natural resource holdings. So it's not even the government that's taking the problem seriously, it's the megacorps."

The robot came back, carrying Jahn's food and water. Jahn picked up the plate of food and put it onto the table. He then picked up the glass of water, and immediately took a sip.

"They're now donating three percent of their revenues to defense, and even colluding to punish companies that don't. Mogna was unwilling to contribute to defense - they said something about corruption, though everyone thought they were just being cheap - and then the charging station makers came together and threatened to lock out Mogna's cars from their grid, ninety percent of charging stations across Freetown, unless they joined in. Yesterday Mogna folded."

"That's ... harsh. If any industry tried that in normal times, they'd get half of Freetown counter-colluding, maybe funding five new competitors against them."

"Normally yes. But hey, times are different now."

Meldan, Veridia

"You off to your first Keeper meeting?", Seila asked Gladias.

"My first two Keeper meetings, back to back. First one is on cultural values in public events and performances - actually the exact one that I judged Dreadknot on way back then."

"Oh, what's the topic for cultural values in events going to be?"

"In the chat I mentioned how I thought the rubric was encouraging people to be too bland to not offend anyone. Surprisingly, a couple others agreed. I think I'll try to make a big push to fix that."

"Veridia ba 'fun' gie!", Seila joked.

"Isn't it the 'gie' that you're supposed to replace? 'fau' just means 'again'."

"Aaah right."

"But yes. Veridia will be fun again."

"What about the second one?"

"The hardware openness rubric. The topic is whether or not to modify it to exempt military and surveillance products."

"Huh, what are the tradeoffs of that?"

Gladias thought carefully about how to phrase this. He thought for a moment about whether or not he should mention Delwart, but then decided against it.

"Well", he began, "some of the Keepers think we should be staying out of funding war - it's a negative-sum game, if both sides have better bombs and battle drones, the result is the same, just more things get blown up and more people get hurt."

He was pleased with himself. He had a feeling that Seila might be sensitive about anything that could hurt Dzego, and would plead for him to take whatever position benefited Dzego the most. He braced himself, preparing for Seila's next question.

"But, funding ... isn't that more of an issue on the Graph Funding side?"

Gladias internally sighed with relief.

"Well remember, we make some weapons too. Also surveillance products. And the rubrics influence how much of the secret sauce we keep to ourselves."

"I see..."

"Well, tell me how the meetings go!"

Gladias walked down a hallway, and entered a courtyard. He found a series of booths with thick sliding doors. He went to the rightmost one, as he had been instructed.

He slid the barrier open. It took a significant effort for him to do so. He could tell immediately that this was a much more proper booth than the cloth-covered booths from the Greater Plum Harbor. As the barrier was opening, he could see its internal structure: a layer of anti-transmission foil on the inside, followed by layers of soundproofing, and other layers he could not recognize.

At that moment, he also noticed a constant humming sound that was being emitted from the outside of the booth on all sides. White noise to further mask anything that makes it through the soundproof walls, he realized. If the noise is at forty decibels and the walls are good enough to attenuate sound by fifty, then it can mask up to ninety decibels coming from the inside - perhaps seventy if you want a safety margin. That's enough to completely mask any conversation.

After fully opening the barrier, Gladias looked inside the booth. There was a table stretching from near the entrance to the opposite wall, and a long bench on each side.

There were five others already sitting down, all wearing privacy robes.

"Welcome! You must be number Four", one of them exclaimed.

"Indeed I am."

"I'm number Twenty in this circle, a third-year. We have two second-years - though Eleven has not arrived yet - two third-years, two other first-years, and now also you."

"Glad to meet you all."

Gladias sat down on the bench beside Twenty. Twenty had his hand device open, and Gladias could see him scrolling through recent audits measuring various businesses' statuses on the cultural values rubric, and the resulting decisions.

A few moments later, another Keeper walked in. He slid the barrier shut behind him, and sat down.

"So, cultural values rubric", the other third-year began.

"Cultural values in events and performances rubric", the first-year, One, corrected. "We're not doing social media or other online things, that's a different rubric. And we're not doing architecture and public billboards, that goes into the aesthetics taxes."

"We all know that, you don't have to show off here", the third-year replied, with a joking tone calibrated to try to make the point without offending One.

"How do we want to do this? Maybe we should first come to a common understanding of what the problems we're trying to solve are?"

"Let's go through some examples", a second year who had not yet spoken up replied.

Gladias saw his chance to intervene.

"How do you guys feel about Dreadknot?"

"What do you mean?"

"Their taxes got bumped up to tier 4 in the last audit."

Gladias began to read from the rubric.

"Content weakly promotes one or more of the following: violence, lawless behavior, use of anti-recommended substances, gambling or risky investment, excessive display of wealth, poor conflict resolution practices, religious or ethnic hatred."

"Do we think Dreadknot is guilty of promoting violence, lawless behavior or hatred?"

"Their last song was about destroying cities and flaying people's flesh. Why not?"

"Do we really think that those words are going to make anyone want to flay anyone's flesh in real life? It's a song. I remember we went through this with games a few years ago, and the science ended up saying that they can slightly increase a few aggressive behaviors but there's no evidence that they actually lead to violence."

"I remember that too. And my read was that the conclusion of the evidence was harsher than that."

"Do we want to dig up and go through those studies together?"

A few other Keepers nodded. They started whispering instructions at their hand devices.

Gladias took the opportunity to continue.

"But even aside from all that, do we really want Veridia to be a society where the artists have to constantly worry about this and all the songs, and the games, and the movies, become boring and pale?"

"They don't have to constantly worry. That's the whole point of Veridia's system of regulation. We're not banning them. We're just setting their taxes slightly higher instead of slightly lower. So along with the ten things that they have to worry about a medium amount already, like what their fans will like, what might or might not offend their corporate sponsors, and so on - things that won't break them, but still make a difference - we ask them to think about one extra concern: the public interest."

Gladias decided to pursue another line of argument.

"I actually like this rubric in general. I think it's great that the Northglade Science Center is getting rewarded for being such a wonderful place for kids to learn about chemistry and biology and rockets."

"But violence is part of life. The human race started out as monkeys fighting over bananas. When we were still living in forests and caves, a quarter of our men died because someone else killed them. The epic poems they make us study and memorize in schools have violence. Every hero of every Great Book did something violent. I don't think we should be discouraging Veridians completely from engaging with such a central part of our human nature. If we steer the public media away from violence everywhere and always, people will get all their ideas about violence from the dark corners of the internet, where nobody gets taxed, and that will be even worse."

"Are there any studies that try to measure this?", Twenty interjected.

"I don't know if you can measure this with studies", Gladias replied.

The other third-year again began to speak.

"This is good, I feel like we've already surfaced some important questions about not just the science, but also our underlying goals and values."

"I think we should re-read the studies from back then about games. But also, we should see what the Veridian people think about this. Can we get Emerald to do a broad listen report on what people have been saying about Dreadknot on Bluewhale or Silverchat in the past year?"

"I don't think what people say on social media is necessarily a good guide to what's good for people", Eleven interjected.

"Okay, but let's take some time right now to read."

Gladias nodded. A few other Keepers nodded after him.

"Just give me a minute. Bluewhale always resists letting you read messages on their platform in any way other than their interface, I have a few hacks to get around that."

Almost exactly a minute later, a new window appeared on each Keeper's hand device, showing Emerald think in real time as it fetched and took notes on what people were saying about violence and Dreadknot on Bluewhale and Silverchat.

The Keepers all began staring intently at their hand devices - some reading the video game studies, others watching Emerald think.

Gladias was standing outside, and sipping a cup of warm water. His first Keeper meeting, seventy-five minutes long, had finished, and he was taking the twenty-five minute break.

His watch buzzed.


From Message Time
Personal reminders
 → Next Keeper meeting starts in five minutes. 39500

It was time to go.

Gladias turned the corner and walked the last few steps toward the booth.

He soon arrived, and slid the barrier open.

There were two other Keepers already sitting inside, one on each side. Both were wearing privacy robes, with their hoods and face coverings still on.

"Hello to you both!"

"Hello! I'm Eighteen. Which number are you?"

"I'm Six."

"And I'm Nine."

Eighteen thought for a few moments, and then stood up.

"Wait, before anyone else comes here, would you all mind standing up again?"

Gladias and Nine both stood up, and briefly exited the booth and looked in from the outside, with the door open.

"Alright, let's take a look."

Eighteen switched his hand device to a different mode, and began waving it around the room. He also took out a drone, and pressed a few buttons on his hand device. The drone began flying around the room near the edges, both above and below the table.

Eighteen and Nine watched silently as Eighteen did his scan, and two more Keepers arrived and quietly joined them.

"Hmm, nothing transmitting, not picking up any powered electronics with thermal either."

A minute later, the drone beeped unexpectedly just above the middle of the table at the far end.

Eighteen jumped to that position with his hand device, and started looking and poking at the table intensely. A few moments later, he stood up triumphantly holding up in his hand a needle-like device, with a bulb a few millimeters wide at its tip.

"What is that?", Gladias asked.

"Spying device. There was a small bump on the table, and this was under it. Definitely takes some skill to insert one of these and then fix up the table this well afterward.", Eighteen replied.

"Wow."

Nine stepped forward and looked at the device briefly.

"I doubt it was meant against us", he said. "Normally, the goal of people who do this is to get information about upcoming business decisions, and trade based on that in the financial markets. Usually, smaller businesses who are less careful. The Order is quite safe against this. Our Keeper group is only one of three discussion groups, so even if you do overhear us all you're only getting one third of the perspective. And we're all speaking through our neck bands so the sound is going between us digitally."

"Actually this one had a camera. It can read your lips and your neck, so there might still be enough information to pick up some words, especially if you're a beginner."

"How do you know?"

"That's how the drone detected it, infrared light reflected off the camera lens. My hand device caught it too with the nonlinear junction detector, but I may well have missed it if the drone did not tell me where to look."

The last two Keepers arrived.

Eighteen stepped out, explained the situation, and the group looked at the listening device together. A few Keepers scanned it with their hand devices. When they were done, Eighteen snapped the listening device in half.

Eighteen led the group to another open booth a few meters away, and slid the booth door open.

He spent two minutes checking the new booth for bugs, again using both his own hand device and his drone. Once he was done, he motioned with his hand, and all seven Keepers entered and sat down on the benches.

One of the newly-arrived Keepers cleared his throat, as though preparing to speak.

"Maybe let's get to business?", the Keeper asked.

"Sure!", Gladias replied.

"So we're supposed to be talking about the openness rubric, and how to adjust it for military hardware."

"Yep, I read the docs."

"And I've had some conversations with Zero over there. His argument is that we should just exempt military hardware completely. I'll let him explain why."

Zero heard his number, and quickly raised his head.

"So normally, open hardware is good, because other people can build on it, and everyone benefits, right?"

"Right."

"But think about what happens with anything military. There isn't actually a net benefit to the world from everyone having better weapons. If everyone has twice as good swords and twice as good shields, the two cancel out."

"If everyone has twice as good swords but shields stay the same, then the benefits to the two sides in any war still cancel out, but more people get hurt."

"But if everyone has twice as good shields but swords stay the same, isn't that good?"

"Well, maybe", Nine interjected. "But actually it's even more complicated than that. What if it's a war of attrition, so if everyone has more defense, the same number of people get hurt, it just takes longer? Or what if increasing defense reduces deterrence, so more wars happen?"

Gladias was surprised: the argument was eerily similar to an argument that Delwart had expressed to him recently.

"Basically, the game tree is just so chaotic that we can't reliably be sure of anything at all. So I think we should just stay out. And instead just increase Steering taxes on all military hardware, open or not, push people to make more useful and pro-human and fun things instead."

A third-year interjected:

"I don't think it's true that we can't be sure of anything. Look at the United Cities. I think it's pretty clear that a big reason they all managed to stay independent from each other for centuries, and figured out things like co-governance to nudge each other to cooperate better without just turning into one big blob, is that they have so many mountains and peninsulas on their continent. So if everyone has more defense, more people can keep their freedom and sovereignty. I think we can be quite confident of that."

Eighteen raised his hand again. The others turned to him, and he began to speak.

"I don't think we can look at the situation like it's a black box like that. Let's look at where we are now. The Arctic Empire's technology is the most advanced. Ours is second. On military tech, Dzego and the United Cities are furthest behind."

"And so when we release open-source military-relevant anything, it doesn't benefit the Arctics at all, and it's marginally good for us because it makes it easier for us to make more."

"But for Dzego, it's a lifeline. They're not set up to invent their own proprietary stuff at the top end, but they're really good at building and adapting from open-source plans. Twenty years ago, when we got our programming languages and formal verification to the point where our devices basically stopped having critical errors in their code that could let someone take it over from the outside, the fact that it was open allowed the Dzegojan to adopt those techniques, and protect themselves much better from Arctic sabotage."

"But do we really want to play this game", Zero continued, "being so confident in our view of who's good and who's bad? Computer security was defensive, fine. But the next technology we invent might be offensive. Won't we just accelerate the arms race even more for everyone?"

"I'm not even that convinced the Arctics are that big a threat. Sure, they're waving more drones around the northern United Cities now, but I don't think the intention is to attack, I think they're just trying to impress us with their power so we become attracted to their ideology."

"Do you think we should be more receptive to their ideology?"

"I think we should keep an open mind. Just remember, the Dzegojan are definitely trying to manipulate us too."

For a few moments, the discussion went quiet. Gladias let it rest. He was still trying to understand how everyone else was thinking before forming his own views.

"Let's all think about this more on our own. We'll keep talking about this, we still have a few more discussions, the last one is in four months. And then the actual vote is only in six months."

Pafogai Du, Dzego

Bai and Zei sat together at a courtyard table, both staring at their hand devices.

"Fin not joining us this time?", Bai asked.

"No", Zei replied with a strong hint of disappointment. "He's busy with the Bansunpei."

The hand devices buzzed. It was their intervention turn. Zei arranged a few gliders and symbol-carrying spaceships. A few hundred turns passed.

Suddenly, as the spaceship hit a rock formation and was in the process of reflecting, gliders from Bai hit it. The spaceship exploded into a storm of gliders.

"What?", Zei shouted.

"Caught you, I had a symbol along the path, right in the position where you could not see it. So I could see the edge of your spaceship coming."

Zei groaned. That had been his last-ditch attempt to rescue the game. More gliders from Bai came in, and shredded through both of his remaining symbols in the southwest corner.

Zei clicked a button to resign.

"Good game", Zei said, not yet with total sincerity, but with more sincerity than he had in any game where he had lost to Bai before.

"You know, I am going to need your help in the nationals."

"Happy to. As long as..."

"Yes, I know, you want to visit Veridia now."

"Anyway, thanks for explaining your thought process in that championship game. Really made me think."

"Of course."

"Of course you enjoy reliving the moment you defeated me, just like I enjoyed beating you right now."

Zei sighed.

"Anyway, I have to go. The Kungaupei councilor, Den, is asking to see me again."

Zei entered the long room, and immediately saw Den and Mu sitting on the other side.

"Thank you for coming."

"Of course. I went through the hash-based signatures you recommended. It's a really fun set of constructions, especially the stateless tree-of-tree-based ones."

"Do you see why, when I looked at your style of Minpentai, I knew that you would do well in this?"

"I think so!"

"You are truly amazing. You've rushed through a third of the cryptography lectures in less than a month, and got a perfect score on both of the first two tests. I can't think of anyone who did better."

Zei's eyes gleamed with satisfaction at receiving the compliment.

"Zei, do you know why I called you in?"

At this point, Zei realized one possible implication of Den's words, and his cheerful facial expression suddenly dropped into a fearful one.

"Are you going to convince me to go into this full-time? Like, abandon the Minpentai nationals?"

Mu laughed. "So I guess my hunch was wrong - this part, you still don't get."

"Huh?"

"Have you ever thought about why the Minpentai game is so serious, so much ceremony, the priests going into the dungeon for days, and so well-funded?"

"It's a sport. Sports are taken seriously and well-funded in many countries."

"Not sports of the mind. Their audience isn't large enough to fund it just based on advertising and national prestige and all those other reasons."

"So why then?"

Mu leaned forward.

"It's because Minpentai isn't just a sport."

Zei stared.

"It's military training."

"The whole point of the sport, and why we support it so much, is to raise the next generation of defenders."

"We need people who can think quickly, and think strategically under pressure."

"People who can compete with their foes, but also cooperate with their allies, even allies that they do not personally get along with."

"People who can understand a battlefield, including the battle itself, all the way up to grand strategy and resources and logistics, and all the way down to the level of surveillance and secrecy and trickery, and ultimately entropy itself."

"People who can deal with suddenly changing rules."

"People who are able to micromanage, but are also able to set a plan in motion and watch it unfold."

"And people who can work with the latest technology - including AI - but also understand and work around its limits."

The realizations hit Zei all at once. At first, he had wanted to ask a basic question: why pretend it's a game, why not just have a regular military with regular recruitment? But as soon as he put together the question, he already knew the answer: the Arctics would put all their energy into targeting anything like that. Minpentai was only safe because it pretended to be just a game. But even then, Zei knew, the ruse could not be safe forever.

"Why are you telling me this now?"

"Because we have to give you some reason why we're now telling you to work hard on cryptography and continue to the nationals. If we didn't tell you, you might get suspicious, eventually figure it out for yourself, and then do something stupid, like excitedly blurting out your discovery to a dozen other people."

Zei nodded.

"I won't tell anyone. Not even Fin."

Den and Mu nodded.

"And when the nationals come, you'll want a sparring partner who knows your style."

No one said a name. No one had to.

"We appreciate your support", Den replied.

"Dze go ba fau gie", Mu added.

"Dze go ba fau gie."

Seila, Daia and Vil were standing together in a large grass field, with many other families nearby.

"Happy to see you here!", Daia exclaimed.

"So how have you been?"

"Well, lots of Order business. Can't talk about it publicly, you know. Going well though!"

"How about you?"

"Well, lots of documents for the lawsuit against Divergent. It's been taking up a big part of my time for the last two months."

"Remind me, what happened there?"

"Ah sorry, I've been trying not to burden you guys with the details, I know you have so much on your plate already."

"Come on, Vil, your life is important to us."

"Well, remember about half a year ago I lost my job at Jump because they went bankrupt. A month later, another one of the employees reached out to me, and I learned from him what really happened. See, the official story had been-"

"I remember this in the news. Jump was struggling, and as a last-ditch effort to save themselves, they made a risky bet on the financial markets, buying a derivative on property prices in a region that they were about to announce they would start serving. But it didn't work - not enough people cared, then they got unlucky and prices went down, so the whole thing collapsed."

"Exactly. But here's what I learned. The only reason why Jump was able to make such a large bet on a niche market without insane slippage is that a hedge fund - Divergent - had taken the other side of the bet. And the primary owners of Divergent had quietly bought a majority share in Jump for very cheap."

"If housing prices in that region had gone up, Jump would have gained, Divergent would have lost, for them it would have been a net zero. And if housing prices went down - which they did - Jump loses, and Divergent gains, also a net zero. But here's the asymmetry: if Jump loses - which they did - then Jump declares bankruptcy, and so they get out of paying end-of-year bonuses plus a year of severance for their employees. So they gave themselves a free option on our backs."

"When we found out about this, we sued - all the employees together sued, as a class action. It's been tough; Divergent even managed to intimidate some media sites into not covering it. But I feel like so far the judges are seeing through their tricks. So I'm optimistic."

Some personal copters, simple chairs with rotor blades on top surrounded by shielding, automatically rolled out of the truck.

Some children, around ten to twelve years old, ran toward the truck, half wearing yellow shirts and the other half wearing purple shirts. Among those wearing yellow shirts was Zven. They grabbed their copters and began strapping into them.

The instructor walked into the truck, and soon came out with a much smaller box. He opened the box, and four bright red drones, shaped like balls a few centimeters wide with soft feather-like rotors on top, sprang out and flew into the sky.

"Welcome to today's Helisport game", the instructor said. "Today we're going to do a limited game, playing only with redballs. If you catch a redball, bring it back to me, and your team gets one point. First team to get to six points wins."

By this point all ten children had strapped into their personal copters, and the rotor blades were beginning to spin - just enough to overcome about three quarters of the earth's gravity. The kids ran around excitedly, and some jumped, reaching about two meters off the ground before gently gliding back down.

"Everyone know what to do?", the instructor asked.

"Yes!", many kids shouted in unison.

"Then we will begin the game in five ... four ... three ... two ... one ... blast off!"

The personal copters flew into the air.

"You know, I'm surprised they still do this in schools", Gladias said to Seila. "If this were invented today, they would definitely say it's too dangerous."

"It was only invented less than ten years ago."

"In Dzego."

Zven caught sight of a redball, and began flying toward it. A few moments after, two kids wearing purple shirts also saw the redball, and began to chase it right behind him.

The redball suddenly shifted direction to the left.

Zven and the other kids also turned left. Zven's copter's rotor shield bumped into the rotor shield of one of the other kids' copters, and the two bounced harmlessly off each other.

Zven aimed his copter to fly higher. He fell slightly behind the kid he had just bumped into, while the third kid flew forward, and was soon directly under him. The air sucked Zven down, and soon his feet bounced into the grid on top of the other copter's rotors.

Zven jumped off quickly, and he and the other kid both tumbled down a few meters before they stabilized and flew off in separate directions.

The instructor watched Zven land, and stretched out his hand to receive the redball that Zven handed over.

Zven flew back up, and continued his search for more redballs.

"How are Hreda, Lily and Febric doing?", Gladias asked Daia. Seila heard the question, and turned her head toward them slightly to hear the answer.

Zven continued his solitary quest to search for the fourth redball, which all the other kids seemed to have completely forgotten the existence of.

"Nice catch by Egardo! Fifth point for team purple."

Meanwhile, out of nowhere, Zven seemed to fall to the ground, the fall broken as usual by the copter's AI.

sa dzu du

ti ka dia shu fe cen su jui hui

An alarm buzzed.

Zei tapped on his watch to check what time it was. 30,003, the watch said. Only half a longhour before the commencement ceremony. He tapped a few buttons on the room service menu, and ordered a fruit and vegetable juice.

He put on his clothes.

Three minutes later, the juice arrived, and Zei quickly drank it. He immediately felt energized - or at least, energized enough to take the trip to the venue.

Without wasting any more time, he opened the door, and went downstairs.

A black car was already waiting for him. Zei walked through the lobby, and immediately stepped through the hotel door and car door that were already open and pressed tightly against each other. The door closed.

As the car began to move, Zei took out the cryptography textbook that Den had recommended to him in one of their meetings, and continued reading it where he had left off.

The section was on hash functions. In the middle of the page, there was a large diagram.



"Conception of a hash algorithm".

Zei read the accompanying text.

Hash algorithms, it said, were there to create a shrunken fingerprint of a large piece of information, that still uniquely identifies the original. The goal is for it to be infeasibly hard to find two different pieces of data that have the same hash.

Hashes inherently destroy information - representing a larger thing with a smaller thing is their entire goal. But there is a paradox: in the internal workings of all the best hash functions that we build, the largest component is an entropy-preserving transformation: a permutation.

The core building block maps inputs to outputs one-to-one. And not only that, it can be efficiently run both forwards and backwards. The shrinking, and the irreversibility, comes from a simple layer on top: a deletion, and an xor of part of the original input, added to the end.

Why do this? Why build irreversibility on top of reversibility? The reason is subtle. If you build irreversibility directly, then you cannot control when entropy is destroyed. If you apply an irreversible round function enough times, then about half the entropy collapses, bringing the protocol's security down along with it. And so even when destroying information is your final goal, it's best to cleanly separate out the piece that's going that - destroy information in one precise spot in the algorithm, on your own terms.

Zei put away his hand device, and leaned back.

It's all entropy, isn't it, he thought to himself.

A minute later, the car suddenly slowed down, and turned left. To his right, Zei could see an area blocked off by safety tape with various large vehicles further inside.

"What happened?", Zei asked in a voice loud enough that the driver would unambiguously recognize that the question was meant for him.

"Explosion in an advanced biology research lab. Probably the Arctics, as usual. They're going to spend days cleaning up to make sure everything is safe."

A few minutes after that, the car slowed down and came to a stop. The door opened, leading straight into a hallway.

Zei walked through the tunnel, and down the stairs.

He saw a door in front of him. The door looked similar to the door to the Minpentai room inside the mountain pyramid in Pafogai Du: a series of stone bricks, curving near the top into an arch, and the symbol at the top: two horizontal arms, meeting in the middle with clashing fists.

However, this door was noticeably larger, more well-maintained, and the decorations more grand.

Zei tapped his watch against the green circle, and the door opened. He walked through.

He entered a room with about fifty chairs, with about twenty contestants already sitting down. On the stage, he recognized Su. Beside her, there were three other priests.

Zei sat down. Over the next fifteen minutes, other contestants sat down in their own chairs.

An older teenage boy sat down beside Zei.

"Hi, I'm Deluin", he said.

That's not a very Dzegojan name, Zei thought.

"I'm Zei."

"Where are you from?"

"Ah, I'm from Redshire. My name gave me away, didn't it?"

Zei laughed. "Do you get that reaction from everyone?"

Deluin laughed along with Zei.

"De lu hin, they call me here. 'A fork with the appearance of'. Lovely name, don't you think?"

"Are you studying here? Did your parents immigrate?"

"Ah, I'm a foreign contestant. They brought in four foreign contestants this time, to make things more fun."

"Are you excited?"

"Absolutely. Actually my first time in Dzego, super cool place."

A bell rang, and the contestants quickly quieted down.

"Welcome to the national Minpentai championship", Su began. "I am honored to see so many brilliant contestants this year, and I hope that everyone arriving had a good evening and a good morning."

"I am pleased to introduce our lead organizer, Taskmaster Jin."

One of the other priests stepped forward, and began speaking.

"This is a special moment for all of us in Dzego, not just for us and for you, but for millions of Dzegojan who watch the games from across the country, as they will get to watch the brightest minds from Dzego's new generation face off against each other."

"I'm also honored to announce that this year, we have four distinguished foreign guests participating along with us."

"Today, we will have a walk through the Minpentai museum, right here inside this mountain pyramid. Tomorrow, we will have some tourist excursions around Sadzu Du, and in the evening you will get a chance to rest. Two days after, the first championship games will begin."

"There will be six rounds of qualifying games, with an eight-day-long break in between each game."

"Out of the thirty-two of you, the four players who win the most games will advance to the semifinals. If there is no win threshold that exactly four players pass, we will break ties by the geometric average of the number of turns that you survived before losing your losing games and the inverse of the number of turns that you needed to win your winning games, counted up to a maximum of eight thousand turns. Thus, there is no incentive to resign before eight thousand turns. If there are still ties, we will insert an additional qualifying round."

"I hope you can enjoy the games, enjoy everything that Sadzu Du has to offer, but also, just as importantly, enjoy each other. Here you are not enemies, you are temporary competitors. Off the arena, you should consider each other friends, and remember that we are all part of a shared project together. Dze go ba fau gie."

"Dze go ba fau gie", all the contestants replied in unison.

"Now, please follow Su. She will lead the excursion through the museum."

Zei began by quickly drawing random junk in his sandbox, seeing what stayed stable and what turned into a glider. Within one minute, he identified a few gliders and a few static structures that could be used for walls. To his surprise, the gliders that moved the fastest moved ... directly east.

His next move was to deliberately draw different kinds of walls, fly gliders at them, and see what sticks.

He watched the gliders carefully, to try to quickly get an intuition for what kinds of shapes can move while preserving their shape. He did several rounds of defining both the gliders and the walls.

"PA MU GU GU GEI TAU FA." The battle begins in fifteen hundred ticks.

Zei began experimenting with shapes that were similar to his symbol, seeing if any of them could function as a glider. He needed to come up with something - otherwise he would be able to progress only very slowly, by repeatedly building a new symbol beside his existing symbol during each intervention turn.

He realized that to make actual headway, he would need to interact with the rock formations. He made a couple of guesses about what shape the rock formations in the hexgrid version of Minpentai might look like, and examined the behavior of gliders as they crashed into them.

"FI SHI GEI TAU FA." The battle begins in a thousand ticks.

He thought more about the exact shape of his symbol.

After another two minutes of fruitless exploration, Zei's mind flashed back to the textbook he had been reading less than two longhours before.

The core building block maps inputs to outputs one-to-one. And not only that, it can be efficiently run both forwards and backwards.

But unlike the hash function, here there was no truncate-and-xor wrapper at the end. And so if he knew his desired end state ... he just had to put that end state into the sandbox, and play it backwards.

But ... how do you play it backwards?

In the internal permutation of a hash function, you walk backwards from the last layer to the first layer, and invert each step as you go.

Here ... what was the inverse of the hexgrid rules that Zei was interacting with for the first time in his life?

Zei took the gliders he saw, and tried the most basic transformations: flipping them, rotating them 60 degrees, launching them one timestep later. None worked.

"MU FI LE GEI TAU FA." The battle begins in five hundred ticks.

Zei stepped through each step more slowly. And then he saw it. During each step, the game board split up into triangles, and the hexagons rotated inside each triangle - clockwise if it had one hex filled, counterclockwise if it had two hexes filled.

And so in order to time reverse, he just had to ... let each time step happen twice. The opposite of a 120-degree rotation is, after all, two 120-degree rotations. But there was a problem: after each time step, the split into triangles shifted. So to play a time step backward, he had to... play one step forward, then shift time back one step so that he could play the next step forward under the same tiling, then play a second step forward to bring the total rotation under that tiling to 240 degrees within each triangle, then shift time back two steps so that the game would shift to the previous tiling. Invert each step, and play the steps in reverse order, just like inverting a permutation in a hash.

He confirmed: there was a button to play one step forward, and two buttons to shift time - either forward or backward. So that's what he would have to do. A, B, A, B, B. Like some kind of video game cheat code. Which, in some sense, here it literally was.

Fine, he thought.

He put a glider into the sandbox, and tried it. It was an arduous process, and his fingers quickly tired. But it worked. The glider moved backwards.

He tried again, with a different glider. This time, it succeeded. As time moved backwards, past the moment of the crash, the rock-formation-plus-symbol turned into a bare rock formation, and two gliders flew back out.

"FI LE GEI TAU FA." The battle begins in one hundred ticks.

Zei quickly repeated the same experiment with other candidates for a rock formation. He paid no attention to the voice announcing the countdown, and kept trying until he found one for the two other most natural options.

"MU GU GEI TAU FA."

Zei quickly put up symbols, walls, and gliders that would create symbols if they crashed into favorable rock formations.

He was surprised at his own speed doing this, given how much longer everything else had taken. But almost immediately he realized in the back of his mind that this made sense: figuring out what to deploy is the hard part, deployment is just copy and paste.

After making a basic setup on the board, he breathed out. Just as he breathed back in and started doing a final pass refining his structures, a final countdown began.

"PA GU ... SO ... BI ... ZE ... HA ... MU ... FO ... SHI ... LE ... PA ..."

"TAU FA."

Gliders started flying out. At first, nothing happened.

Five hundred turns later, a part of the board came into view. One of his gliders had successfully created a symbol, and revealed a part of the board that showed what the rock formations look like.

Immediately, Zei switched to the next task: figuring out how to build glider factories.

When the first intervention turn hit, Zei had not yet figured this out. However, he did send out several more gliders that flew from his home base, ready to create more copies of his symbol if they collided into a rock formation in the right place. He also sent gliders from nearby his new symbol, rapidly heading east.

The audience watched intently. From across the river, Bai was also watching intently. And from afar, so were Fin, Mu and Den.



The audience was surprised. Neither player had managed to figure out any gliders that move vertically, they realized.

On the second intervention turn, Zei launched gliders from the sides of the board, aiming straight toward Bo's home base.

And just before the third intervention turn, one of Zei's gliders hit a rock formation right beside Bo's home base, allowing Zei to see all of Bo's symbols.

Zei used that intervention turn to send gliders directly toward the three of Bo's symbols that he could see, and more toward some locations nearby just in case.

Within three hundred turns, all of Bo's symbols were destroyed, and Zei was announced the winner.
