Zei immediately forwarded the note to Bai. He also sent a copy to Fin, and sent Emerald an instruction to send Fin a maximum-priority emergency alarm and an explanation of what was going on.

Fin responded almost immediately.

"Alright Zei, what do you need?"

"Reading..."

"Yeah this seems doable. It's a not very well known fact that you don't actually need the raw weights of a model to effectively train adversarial attacks. There's definitely Bansunpei people who are very good at this stuff - 'language models' are quite connected to language!"

Zei also forwarded the note to Mu. Emerald automatically formed a real-time chat group. After a minute, about ten people were sharing insights about the problem and beginning to attack it in parallel.

"Let's assume that our attack medium is that we have our snow drones, and we have stick-on paper that we can print things on. We'll assume we deploy this after sunrise. Here's what you do: start with one pattern, run it inside the simulator, have our drone slowly approach the target and see how long it takes for the target to detect it. Measure detection time so that we have a scalar signal of how well we're hiding, not just a binary."

"Continue making small modifications to the pattern in all kinds of directions. Keep each modification that increases the target's detection time. It doesn't matter if the process has a lot of noise, the signal accumulates and the noise averages out over time. It's not as fast as gradient descent, but it still works. Eventually you get to a pattern that reliably tricks the adversary."

"We can do better. We have our own models that were trained in similar ways to the Arctic ones, and we obviously have the raw weights to those. So we can use gradient descent against our model. Identify, say, ten optimal perpendicular directions that maximize time-to-detection according to our model inside our simulator, and then use those as the trial deviations we try against their model inside their simulator. Simultaneously, we also use the results of every query to fine-tune our model to make it a better predictor of how the Arctic model will behave on these attacks."

"How quickly can we get this working?", Zei interjected.

"Coding should take at most ten minutes, Emerald can do it quickly. The full training loop ... maybe a longhour?"

"So it will be done around sunrise?"

"Exactly. And then you will need I don't know how many minutes to actually print the attack patterns on the sides of the drones, you should prepare that pipeline on your side so it's ready to go as soon as we are."

"Alright, everyone. Let's get moving."

Zei sat back, and kept scanning through zoomed-in views of the battle map and visual feeds. About a third of the Veridian drone fleet was already lost, but casualty rates had decreased considerably. The slow retreat strategy was working well: it also meant that any Veridian drones that had motion disabled by combat damage but had their weapons still intact could go into low-power mode and then wake up and do a final burst of damage as soon as the Arctics themselves advanced to their position.

After about fifteen minutes, Zei's watch buzzed again. Emerald was telling him to rejoin the chat.

"We have some early good news", a Bansunpei researcher exclaimed.

"What is it?"

"We've successfully accessed the Arctic simulation platform, and we've run the first few hundred trial rounds against the simulator. We have patterns that are increasing detection time by about five percent."

"Only five percent?"

"That just means the pipeline is starting to work."

"Oh, it just went up to eleven percent."

"It's definitely working", another researcher interjected. "We're continuing to run Emerald in parallel, optimizing the software. It's finding ways to extract more information from each query, and better parallelize the queries so this all happens faster."

Zei's watch buzzed.


I can see you are starting to run queries! Though you want to be more careful - if I can see it, the sentries might be able to as well. Here are some more proxy endpoints.

Also, add a bunch of dummy queries that are doing other things, and maybe even make each query attempt multiple different attacks simultaneously so it's less clear what it's doing.


Good advice, Zei thought. He forwarded it.

To verify the effectiveness of the simulator, they also ran simulations in a nighttime environment that exactly replicated a real-world setting of a small battle that had taken place earlier in the night. Another team, two researchers and Emerald instances, began figuring out how to automatically analyze the discrepancies between the simulator and reality in the nighttime setting to learn how to construct queries to the simulator that would better match real-world situations.

Zei watched the attack patterns become more and more optimized, sheets of paper containing squiggles and messages that seemed simultaneously very recognizable and familiar but also completely alien. Inside the simulator, the time that it took for the Arctic drone AI to detect their incoming drones more than doubled.

After another thirty minutes, it doubled again.

Lektor gave the order to set up printing infrastructure about two kilometers behind their current positions - a place they would be able to safely organize a retreat to around sunrise.

Human Veridian soldiers were already tens of kilometers behind the robotic frontline, and Lektor ordered them to start moving toward the front, so that they would be available to paste the attack patterns onto the snow drones. Manual dexterity was still a major weakness of AI.

Slowly, the sky began to shift from a near-total pitch black to a dark blue that was especially visible in the far east. As the minutes passed, the blue became brighter.

"Alright, we have some good patterns. It's getting close to sunrise in Northshore. I recommend shipping them now."

"Agreed", Zei replied.

"Then let's do it", Mu added.

Zei flipped through the visual feeds in his display. The majority of their drone fleet had retreated a kilometer, and a large number of pieces of paper were being printed and then almost immediately getting distributed and then stuck onto all sides of each snow drone and sky drone. The plan was in motion.

"Group North reporting: all non-forward drones have been equipped."

"Group Center reporting: all non-forward drones have been equipped."

"Group South reporting: all non-forward drones have been equipped."

"Group Naval reporting: we commandeered equipment in villages on the outskirts of Northglade, the locals were amazing, many woke up in the middle of the night to help us. Most non-forward drones have been equipped."

"Alright then", Lektor spoke up softly but firmly. "Action."

Zei checked the visual feeds, curious what the final version of the attack patterns actually looked like. He saw an endless row of snow drones with large pieces of paper plastered on all sides, each paper containing many colorful and squiggly patterns - and in a giant font, the word "DOG".

A few minutes later, he could see the results. The Veridian snow drones advanced quickly, pushing through enemy lines and turning the front into a chaotic mixture of drones on both sides. Casualty ratios were more than ten to one in the Veridian drone fleet's favor.



Zei allowed himself to feel a moment of joy - the first genuine joy that he had felt the whole night.

He remembered Den's words to him the day that he had almost caused the failure of the mission to rescue the Redshire president's son. "Outside the box as in, jumping out of your console chair and running over and bashing the other player in the face."

Breaking into your opponent's simulation environment, running millions of queries to optimize squiggles that you could draw on a piece of paper, and tricking your opponent's drones into thinking that your drones are dogs - did that count?

It probably did, Zei decided. Den would be proud.

As soon as he felt he had celebrated enough, Zei turned to a visual view of the statistic that really mattered: the casualty ratios. They had already dropped to six to one. So far the Arctic army had not yet adapted, but they had adopted emergency defensive positions, each squad of drones circling into a formation, to buy time. And they would adapt soon, Zei knew.

The chat that contained Bansunpei and Kungaupei members making queries to the Arctic simulation environment switched to optimizing simpler attacks: motion patterns that maximally delayed detection and interfered with targeting, sounds that could trick them, as well as the accuracy of their own fire - all mechanisms that did not require printing and sticking on new pieces of paper. They also incorporated some of the aggressive micro-tactics that Deluin had sent along with his original message.

Casualty ratios briefly increased back in the Veridians' favor, and then started decreasing again, though slowly. Zei continued watching.

After fifteen minutes, all access to the simulation environment was suddenly cut off. At around the same time, casualty ratios suddenly dropped back down to only one and a half to one in the Veridians' favor.

They had destroyed a large part of the Arctic drone fleet, but a large part still remained. They were now in a complicated positional battle, with a chaotic mixture of both sides' drone squads littering the battlefield with no clear front line.

Veridian human soldiers were only hundreds of meters behind the frontline, finding snow drones that were quickly repairable and repairing them. They were wearing thermal cloaks to minimize the chance of detection, and smoke from nearby burning trees provided additional cover. In a few of the visual feeds, Zei could see images of Arctic human soldiers doing the same thing in the distance, but they were far fewer in number: while Veridians had been retreating through the night, they had been laying traps along the way, and those traps were much more effective against humans than against drones.

A few minutes later, Zei's watch buzzed again.


I hope you trust me now.

My next message will contain exact coordinates of some of our units on the southern flank, and recommended weak points to attack through.

jie fe hen dzi.


Zei smiled.

Of course I trust you, Deluin, he thought.

Almost immediately, Zei's watch buzzed again. He had received the second message.

He forwarded the coordinates to Mu.

"It's your chance to shine, Mu."

"Don't forget Vakaria."

Within minutes, casualty ratios on the southern front began to diverge heavily from the fronts further north, going back up in the Veridians' favor.

And only a few minutes later, they seemed to have achieved the result that they needed.



Mu transferred control of the southernmost portion of her drone fleet to Vakaria, who was assigned the task of entering and regaining control of Northglade.

The rest of her drone fleet swept northward. Over the next longhour she managed to completely surround the remaining Arctic drone fleet, linking up with Telpo's northernmost flank almost exactly a longhour after sunrise.

Gallowar's Group North defeated the remaining Arctic drones to its north and reached the river that marked the delineation between Veridian and core Arctic territory. A few drones crossed the river and bolted toward nearby Arctic towns, causing the Arctics to send emergency reinforcements. A portion of Telpo's fleet headed north to join Gallowar, reinforcing the northern front.

In the meantime, the second trip of seaborne drones went directly to Thaldur - the island east of Northshore that was core Arctic territory - and landed a fleet of air and snow drones that consolidated control over the island over the next few longhours. The Arctics could not effectively react, as Thaldur was too far away for either side to reach quickly, and the few drones that were in range were stuck defending against Gallowar.

By late afternoon on that day, the fighting grew quieter, as the last remnants of Arctic soldiers and drones in Northshore and Thaldur were methodically hunted down.

Zei sat back in his chair, and set it to incline backward as far it could. For the first time in over fourteen longhours, he went to sleep.

Chapter 31

Northglade, Veridia·3725 Rainmoon 2

Zei, Bai and Mu slowly walked up the staircase on the side of the mountain. The mountain was fully covered with snow on both sides, and the sunlight reflected off the snow into their eyes. Only pine trees and the staircase with its handrails were visible above the snow - the trees and the handrails because they were too high for the snow to fully cover them, and the staircase itself because it was being regularly plowed and salted by a drone that they could see about thirty meters further above them.

A strong, cold wind blasted into their faces. They continued climbing. Several minutes later, they reached the circular platform at the top of the mountain.

From there, they could see a full view of the island on which Northglade was located. It was about twenty kilometers wide - small enough that the most simplified and highly zoomed out maps of the region did not even bother showing it, but at the same time large enough that it seemed like if it really had to, that island alone would be large enough to sustain a civilization. If Northglade had been a Dzego city, Zei thought, it would have a fully self-sufficient emergency industry already.

To their east, they could see the main city of Northglade. To the west and north, they saw snowy hills for kilometers on end, and a path gently twisting as it descended deeper into the forest. Looking downward to the east, Zei could see another staircase leading up to the summit, and a young man wearing only a sweater and a light hood climbing up.

As he neared the top of the summit, Zei could recognize a familiar face.

"Deluin!", he shouted.

Deluin raised his head up, saw Zei, and ran up the last twenty meters of the staircase.

He reached the top, and almost threw Zei off balance as he threw himself into his arms for a hug.

"I'm so happy you're still alive, Zei, and that I can finally see you again."

Deluin slowly let go of Zei and turned toward Bai.

"Wait, do I recognize you?"

"I'm Bai. You might have seen me watching some of the practice games in Sadzu Du."

"Ah yes, I remember you!", Deluin replied, somewhat unsure if he was genuinely recollecting a memory of seeing her or simply confabulating one.

"And I'm Mu. Don't you dare mix me up with Su - she's still back in Dzego, she's a completely different person from me."

"Nice to meet you, Mu", Deluin replied, gently laughing.

"So tell me. What happened?"

"Well, this is a long story. Are you sure you want it told at the top of a cold snowy mountain?"

Zei, Bai and Mu all immediately nodded in unison.

"I see you're more fit to live in Redshire than I might have expected!"

"Okay fine, I'll start."

"Back in Grapetime, about two months after they occupied Redshire, some Arctic officers came to our house, to talk with my parents. My parents were never particularly worried about the Arctic threat, saying we should be more open to peace and cooperating with them. But once the invasion happened, they quickly flipped to just being full supporters of what the Arctics were doing. Quite a large chunk of the Redshire population did."

"The Arctics offered them a position. They said that they should come to Glasscrown, and advise the top leadership on integration - first of the captured Redshire population, then of Northglade residents and eventually of everyone else that they would conquer."

"I made a big risky decision. I decided I would 'go native' - pretend to be a full-on supporter of the Arctic cause, try to use my parents' reputation together with my own status as a Minpentai champion-"

"I'm the Minpentai champion!", Zei playfully interrupted.

"Only because the game was cancelled and they gave you the title. You never beat me."

"I beat you in the battle two days ago!"

"What was that line from that old poem? mi fu zo de tei ka ciu pin - when I am defeated, I feel like I won?"

"Now you get it!"

"Anyway, I used my parents' reputation and my status as a Minpentai semifinals winner to climb up the hierarchy myself. Within two months they figured out independently that Minpentai was an effective way to train people for modern warfare-"

"Wait, they figured out what Minpentai is for?"

"Wait ... you mean you guys intentionally designed the Minpentai tournaments to train people for defense?"

Zei, Bai and Mu immediately nodded.

"Then no, they definitely did not figure that out. They just figured out that Minpentai happened to be effective for that purpose. And so within three months they put me as one of their top commanders."

"The Arctics are actually quite easy to play, you know."

"What do you mean?"

"Their entire ideology completely de-values alignment, and only values competence. They see top talent as being fungible. People as bots that can just be reallocated by pointing a higher salary at them. They don't really have much of a theory of people having their own motivations, dreaming their own hundred thousand dreams, and how to tell when someone's heart beats together with yours and when they are just pretending. And so if you just say the right slogans, and convince them that you're top talent, they just ... trust you."

"Wow."

"I'm ... actually not surprised", Bai added. "I'm just glad that you managed to play the game better than any of the others did."

"So what are the most interesting things about the Arctic Empire?", Mu quietly asked. "What can we learn from them?"

"Their advancements in technology are real, and they are amazing. The medical treatments that they gave to the residents in Northglade are only a sample. They believe that they have already figured out how to make people live a decade longer, and that they're only accelerating."

"Glasscrown is one of the most fascinating cities I've ever seen. It's beautiful in its own way. It makes you feel like you're living inside of a giant ice crystal. Its tallest tower is a kilometer above ground, and its caverns stretch deep underground."

"They even have rows of pine trees alongside some of the walls. That itself is an impressive feat of engineering: genetic engineering to help the plants better tolerate cold, together with underground heating and cleverly shaped reflective walls to make their environment warmer."

"In the winter, Glasscrown has a month and a half of polar night with no sun. Then, the whole city gets enveloped with the glow of white and blue artificial light."

"Now you sound like you want to go back!"

"Actually, I want something else. I think it's good that the Arctics have built all of this technology - though if I could shut one of the things down, it would be the research on superviruses. But what's dangerous is how they keep everything they make for themselves and don't let anyone else benefit. Even when they gave some of it to the Northgladers, it was on their own terms - you come to our health clinics, you don't get to learn what we are doing to your body, and if you don't want to go back to how you were before, you have to keep coming back to our clinics again and again."

"Instead of science and technology bringing the world together, it's turning one group into a bigger and bigger threat that the rest of the world has to fear more and more."

"But thanks to you, we - we as in all of humanity - have now captured a big pile of their technology. Some that they brought into Northglade. Piles of their military equipment scattered around Elenar Forest. And a bunch on the island of Thaldur, core Arctic territory that has tens of thousands of people living on it."

"So our next step should be to convince as many of them as we can to volunteer, and share their knowledge and expertise voluntarily, and bring the whole world up to at least the frontier that the Arctics have created to keep for themselves."

"Open source - it's not just a good idea, it's the law", Zei replied.

"Exactly. Make the whole world a little bit more like Veridia in that way."

"And then we can play their strategy in reverse. Show the people in Thaldur that they have more calm, more peace and more actual freedom under our way of life, at the same time as having powerful technology. Then perhaps through them, we can convince even more Arctics to join our side."

The conversation paused. Deluin took his turn to walk all around the top of the mountain and enjoy the view of Northglade.

About ten minutes later, Mu spoke up again.

"I got some bad news, Deluin."

"What is it?"

"Freetown defense corps are reporting that the Arctic garrison in Redshire has tripled. They tried some sabotage operations with their drones already on Redshire using the tricks that we discovered during the battle two days ago, but they are mostly failing now."

"They now think that there is basically no chance of us getting Redshire back."

Deluin sighed. An expression of deep sadness filled his eyes.

"Tafindel is recommending that we play a little bit of hardball. Close the borders between Thaldur and the rest of Arctic territory. And then offer a deal. We let anyone who wants to go back to the Arctic Empire go back, and in exchange anyone in Redshire who wants to leave is allowed to leave. They keep Redshire, we keep Thaldur. And then find a beautiful place in Veridia to make a new Redshire."

"Why not just give them the peninsula between here and Thaldur, the one dangling off the eastern end of Northshore? Very beautiful land there."

"I think that should be up to them to decide."

Deluin nodded. "Tafindel is probably right. It's as good an outcome as we're going to get."

The conversation paused once again. All four of them looked toward the east, and enjoyed the view of snowflakes gently falling on every building in the town of Northglade and covering it with thick snow.

Gladias and Seila walked through the large stone gates at the entrance to the Greater Plum Harbor in Northglade. The turnstile gates had been smashed and thrown to the ground to let people freely move in and out, and the administrative staff did not seem to have the heart to enforce any visa rules at that particular time. Two Greater Plum Harbor security guards, wearing purple and grey attire, simply watched the crowds move in and out, and resigned themselves to meeting the fallback objective of preventing any theft and violence.

Seila's watch buzzed. She raised up her hand, and took a look.


From Message Time
Jahn
 → [5 images] 45904

She clicked, and took a look at the pictures. The first three were pictures of people in Freetown in its streets and parks celebrating.

The fourth appeared to be an open public concert hosted in a parking lot. In the background was a giant factory building, on the side of which there was a prominently displayed logo of Ichara - one of the now famous Freetown defense companies.

The last was a picture of Jahn himself taking a selfie with what appeared to be one of the managers who worked at the defense company.

"Are you going to go to Freetown and see Jahn?"

"Actually I was thinking to stay in Northglade another five days or so after you leave, and let him come here. He's always wanted to come see Veridia."

"You should", Gladias replied gently.

They walked forward along the street for about a hundred meters, and then descended down into a tunnel. About two hundred meters later, they turned right and walked up a staircase. At the end of the staircase, there was a door.

Gladias prepared to tap his watch against the green circle on the side of the door, but before he could do so, the door opened on its own.

"Dad!", Lily yelled as she ran up to Gladias and hugged him.

"Lily! I'm so happy you're safe."

Febric and Hreda emerged from another room, and rushed to embrace Gladias and Seila.

"I'm so glad that you are all here together."

"I'm sorry, Mom."

"Don't be. We all made lots of mistakes this past year. We've gotten through it now, and if we need to, we can get through even more. We're a family."

"Is Zven here?"

"Oh, Zven, Vil and Daia are coming tomorrow morning!"

"Amazing! I'm so excited to see Mom!", Hreda exclaimed.

"So how has the Greater Plum Harbor been treating you?", Gladias asked.

"It's been actually quite fun.", Hreda replied. "They did a very good job of organizing education, entertainment, public activities, all kinds of things to keep people happy. They convinced the Arctics to allow food to get droned in, so aside from being a small enclosed space it's been fine."

"We had Arctic food out of curiosity a few times here", Febric added. "They've figured out like a dozen substances that taste like sugar but don't have any calories. They also have protein contraptions that taste like fish and meat. It's not bad! Whatever taste you want with whatever nutrition profile you need, the slogan goes."

Seila lowered her face quietly. She was still not entirely used to having to admit that the Arctic ways of doing things sometimes did actually have upsides and they could learn from them.

"How about I invite some of our new friends", Gladias interjected, "and they can show us what actual properly cooked Dzego food is like?"

"Yay!", Lily shouted.

Febric and Hreda also nodded eagerly.

"Then I'll ask them to come tonight. I have to go out again this afternoon. There's a military funeral for Den and our fallen soldiers at the top of the mountain. Then we can come back down together and enjoy a nice meal."

Lily, Febric and Hreda nodded their heads with excitement.

Chapter 32

Meldan, Veridia·3725 Rainmoon 12

Gladias and Seila walked together along the same path through Kalimar that they had by this point taken hundreds of times. The path was covered with trees and surrounded by stone houses on both sides.

To their left, they saw a man climbing a tall ladder leaning against a tree. Once he reached the top of the ladder, he began unscrewing a security camera that was located there. Once he finished, he unceremoniously threw the camera into a box that was several meters below him on the ground. The throw landed perfectly. Gladias and Seila heard a loud clang as the camera crashed against the dozens of other cameras that were already in the box. The man immediately proceeded to climb down the ladder.

They continued walking. They passed by a store, one that Gladias had remembered seeing hastily replace much of its inventory with emergency preserved food rations only months earlier. This time, the inventory item that took up the front shelves was a particular type of red flower that was native to Northglade, that residents were buying to celebrate the province's liberation.

Taped to the side of the store, there was an advertisement:

We are now offering the freshest of fresh water SEIZED from the CORE TERRITORY of the ARCTIC EMPIRE.

Get the latest Hydrafill water, bottled at the springs of Thaldur, today!

Enjoy the spoils of victory. Buy Hydrafill.

The road transitioned to dense shrubbery, and then to a sky bridge overlooking a busy highway. To the left, they could see a mountain covered with trees. A few apartment buildings about fifteen storeys tall, decorated and shaped like oversized medieval castle towers though with far more windows on the sides, poked up high above the trees.

After crossing the sky bridge, the road transitioned into a tunnel, and Gladias and Seila arrived at a Y-shaped intersection. They turned left, walked forward until the path came back up above ground, and then turned right. Gladias checked his watch for directions. He had never actually walked all the way to parliament before.

Twenty minutes later, they arrived at the large circular building. Gladias tapped his watch against the green circle, and the doors opened. Inside the building, he remembered the directions well. Forward, then right turn, then forward, then third door on the left.

He tapped his watch again, and the door opened.

Verdow and Zei were both sitting inside the office. They both turned their heads toward Gladias and Seila.

"Gladias, Seila, welcome back!", Verdow exclaimed with a warm friendly tone.

"Verdow, good to see you again!"

"Please, please sit down."

A robot slid into the room.

Gladias briefly turned to face the robot. "dia jie fe kai ja cu dze kai lin pan", he told the robot in a deliberately clear tone.

The robot buzzed, and left the room.

"Impressive, Gladias. Even I would not have been able to do that."

Verdow briefly went silent, and then spoke up again.

"Okay, I'm embarrassed. What is dze kai lin pan?"

"Vegetable and rice."

"Ah right, green plant line bread."

"By the way Zei, when are we going to start switching over from meters to lightfeet?"

"Fin tells me the Bansunpei is completely busy on getting Dzego's privacy and security habits fully up to the new standards. In about ten days he and some others are actually going to come here to Veridia, and see if they can help you guys get up to speed on those things too."

"But I guess we don't have to wait for them, if you like lightfeet you can just start using lightfeet today."

"I guess they're right. Switching over to lightfeet isn't the highest priority right now."

Verdow's tone suddenly became more serious.

"A lot of people are celebrating this month. For the first time in a century, the Arctic Empire has been defeated. Northglade is free. And we already have many people in Thaldur taking up our offers and helping open up the Arctic technologies we captured so that we can properly benefit and learn from them."

"But we have to remember - this was only the first round. And even this round, we did not fully win."

"The Arctics lost Northshore and lost Thaldur, but they kept Redshire. They lost some of their lead in technology, but we've learned over the past few months that they are rapidly gaining in other kinds of technology."

Verdow sighed, and then continued giving his cautionary note.

"The privacy that we thought we had, we do not actually have. In the digital world, we're okay - cybersecurity and cryptography are amazing now, though we have to remember that language models will always be attackable in ways that regular software is not. In the physical world, it's much harder. Information in physical reality is fundamentally much more leaky. There are dozens of ways even our keystrokes on our keyboards leak out into the world outside. We can make an effort to fight this - especially in our private spaces - but there's a limit to how much we can succeed."

"I hear there's already a batch of the new cameras from Dzego flying in, with built-in hard guarantees of what information they can and can't transmit. VNU is figuring out the process for inspecting them. They seem to want to just copy the way that Dzego has been doing it."

"Ooh, so that's what it was? We saw someone unscrewing a hundred cameras in Kalimar when we were walking to get here."

"Looks like it."

Gladias decided to change to a different topic.

"What do you think about our government?", he asked Verdow.

"The Order of Steering worked, the Courts worked, Graph Funding has been fine. But everything more transparent has been broken. By default, I expect that everything the government does is going to become even more private going forward. More digital-first, more sealed anti-transmission rooms, more privacy robes."

Verdow sighed, clearly at least somewhat unhappy with the state of affairs that he was predicting.

"There's a fundamental tension here that our system of government has been grappling with since the day it was first created. In an interconnected world, how is it even possible for a government to be accountable to its own citizens, without also being 'accountable' to powerful financial interests on the inside and adversaries on the outside, both of which are trying to press at the weakest point, isolate it and pressure and twist it to serve their own ends?"

"We need to keep improving our theory of what transparency and accountability even mean. In this current iteration of our government, the answer has been the selection process from one end, and Heralds from the other end. In the next iteration, it might have to be something else. I think it will have to involve something like Silverchat polls, or maybe something even higher bandwidth, to understand people's goals, and something involving AI to figure out how to achieve those goals."

"Zei, what do you think?"

"AI is the start of the conversation, not the answer. What kind of AI is it? How do we train it? Who trains it? What instructions do we give it? Who feeds the AI information, and who intervenes in the AI's thought process to assist it?"

"How would you answer that?"

"I would first take a step back and ask what the problems are. And I think I have noticed one. Veridian institutions, as they exist today, don't really have a built-in concept of predicting the future. It's all about the present, and public opinion in the present."

"There's no position where you have to stand up and say - if we do X, then Y will happen - and you rise up if you're right, and fall if you're wrong. The closest is Acolytes, that have to predict the Sentinels. But even there, they're not predicting the real world. They're predicting Sentinels. So they're still just predicting other people's opinions. You've aligning people to each other, but you're not aligning people to reality."

"That's where AI could do very well - it's where AI already has done very well for us. But I don't think we should pick one AI, we should have some kind of open competition of them. AI should be a player, not the game. Let different people choose different AIs and different ways of working with them, and hold them accountable to the goals."

"Should a society have goals?"

Zei stared at Verdow.

"What do you mean?"

"The Arctics are better at having goals than any of our nations. They know exactly what they want, and are single-minded about achieving it. If you make a perfect goal-executing machine, the Arctics are what you get."

"That's why you need the other piece - being able to gather together different people's goals and add them up, so you know that you're achieving the actual goals of the people, and not just one emperor."

"But what if any goal you come up with and write down on a piece of paper ends up looking like that?"

"What do you mean?"

"What if part of the human condition is that we don't fully know what we want, and any attempt to crystallize it into one piece breaks down if you push it far enough? We see this with our rubrics: they work for some time, then eventually they get gamed, and then we adjust the rubrics, and repeat. What if that's unavoidable?"

"Then what's the alternative?"

"Think of a lake, full of water. Every molecule of water in the lake acts independently. There is no master plan. There are only trillions of molecules dreaming trillions of dreams. The lake has a harmony and balance to it, we can all see that. But it's not because anyone forces that balance to happen, it's because if any one part of the lake's surface ends up lower than the other parts for even a brief moment, then gravity will attract water to flow in, and the height everywhere will be the same again."

"But also, when winter comes, the molecules come together, into thick crystalline structures of impenetrable ice."

"You understand physics well."

"My daughter is starting to study chemistry, she has been telling me a lot about it. Her friends think she's over-working, but I've been encouraging her - I told her that if she studies hard, one day she can be just like you."

Zei blushed.

"So that's what I think the ideal is. A society that can do the good of ordinary life but not the evil of empire and conquest. One that can both resist the Arctic Empire, and avoid becoming one, and instead prosper peacefully one step at a time."

"It's hard to agree on what we want, it's easier to agree on what we don't want. I think that's the asymmetry that we build everything on top of. In the winter, we all align in the same direction, and we can form the crystal, and defend and strike back. In the summer, we flow like water. Decentralized forces - markets, open intellectual discourse, open science, culture and law - passively make the trillion forces of our trillion dreams add more often than they subtract. We adjust their rules over time, but only carefully and slowly. The natural, gentle progress we make from decades upon decades of that is worth more than satisfying any goal."

"What if sometimes different parts of the lake have to be water and ice at the same time?"

"That may be."

"And what if a lake where every point is at the exact same height as every other point is also a kind of uniformity that we don't want, and sometimes it's better if we form snowballs and let them float?"

"That too may be."

"Seila, what do you think we should do more?"

"The Arctics have competition - they care about who's better and who's worse, and they encourage people to challenge each other and strive and try to rise to the top - but they do not understand cooperation. They are ice without the water. Veridia has cooperation, but maybe we do not understand competition. We can be water, but we don't yet know how to be ice - and even our water does not always flow as well as we would like. Actually I think it's Dzego that's figured out how to have both, and make them serve each other. We should learn from them more."

She sighed deeply. After a few moments, Verdow replied again.

"These are all good thoughts."

"Zei, would you be interested in staying back and helping us figure out some of these issues?"

Zei thought for a moment.

"I'm sure Mu and Su can handle the Kungaupei well", Gladias interjected.

"Of course! Though you might find Fin will be even more helpful than I am."

"Well I appreciate it. You know, Parliament realizes now that their current ways of thinking have hit their limits. Many senators have resigned. The ones who are still there - like me - we want new ideas. We're open to listening."

Verdow stood up, and walked over slowly to a map of the world that was printed on the side of the office wall.

"This is our world. Ninety million people. Gladias, Seila, Zei, have you ever wondered what things might be like if it was nine hundred million, or nine billion?"

"I have not. Why do you ask?"

"The larger the population, the faster new technologies get invented. That's why the medieval era was so stagnant, and why things are moving so much faster today. But no matter how large the population, everyone still adapts to the technology at the same rate. Maybe we've done so well at adapting - eradicating computer viruses, adding so much privacy and verifiability to everything, optimizing our society to be so beautiful and healthy - only because we don't have nine billion people pushing technology forward even faster and increasing the complexity of the society that has to accept it."

"That's interesting. Do you think we will have nine billion people one day?"

"Not one day. Very soon. And not people. Bots. And not nine billion. Nine trillion."

"That's what I worry about. AI is going to really change everything. So far, progress has been moderate, nobody has lost their jobs, it feels more like everyone has been promoted to being a manager - or sometimes a repairman. But at some point, once the AI can do almost everything that humans can do, even if at a few percent the efficiency, our human population won't be a constraint anymore."

"So what do we do?"

"Well, we don't really have much power to be the ones to answer that question if the Arctics continue to stay further ahead."

"If we want to get back into balance, we have to get better at penetrating them. Have more of a view into their society and their technology, make sure that for any advance they make, we learn about it. Privacy for the weak, transparency for the powerful. Having those people from Thaldur helping us is great, and hopefully Deluin is far from the only person from Redshire who pretended to join the Arctics but would be interested in passing more information to us."

"There's a known result from game theory", Zei interjected. "If two players are locked in a game that has some mixture of cooperation and competition, then you can unlock strictly higher levels of cooperation if those players can at least partially read each others' minds. Maybe that's the right outcome to hope for. As time passes, we'll learn more about each other, we'll learn from each other, and we'll come to actually understand each other better."

"I'm not so optimistic. The Arctic Emperor is upset. He can't do anything to us right now, but he's definitely scheming. There will be a next round. It could be five years from now, it could be twenty years from now. If we can at least keep pace on technology, we can survive."

"Do you think we should try to slow them down?"

"Do the same thing to them that they have been doing to Dzego for a century? It's not the worst idea."

Zei sighed.

"If we were able to keep advancing under their pressure, they'll definitely be able to keep advancing under any pressure we can bring to bear against them."

"You know, the later stages of all this are going to get crazy. At some point, eventually we'll have drones the size of worms and flies burrowing under the ground, flying through the air and swimming under the sea. We'll have new forms of genetically engineered life that we can't even imagine - both for peace and for war. Some of us might be uploaded and living inside computers. Not this year. Not the next few years. But definitely in the next hundred years."

"Maybe in two hundred years it will be stable. We'll have figured out exactly the ideal type of drone at every scale, the largest as large as aeroplanes or even hollowed-out asteroids floating in space, and the smallest so tiny that there's no more gap between them and viruses. Once we hit the ceiling, there would be nothing else even stronger that could defeat them. Just big distributed immune systems protecting our planets, our animals and our trees, and ourselves. We will be wiser, almost everyone will choose peace over war, and those who don't will have no path to impose their will. And everyone will just live the kind of life they want to live."

"I just hope we have peace", Seila added. "All these questions: genetic engineering, uploading, going to the stars, I don't think we can get the right answers if we take every step in a rush because we're scared. I'm not sure I want to upload. But a year ago I was not sure if I wanted to live for more than a hundred years. These things should all be a choice we make carefully, and have respect for people who choose not to take the same choice as we do, not an urgent decision we make to survive in a war."

Verdow rejoined the conversation.

"We might have that peace, we might not. We can hope for the best, but we have to be ready for all possibilities."

"You know, a few days ago Bai mentioned to me that she was thinking of spending a year in Thaldur - precisely to better understand how the Arctics think, and see if she can find a path to that peace."

"That sounds a lot less scary than what Deluin did. I support her."

The door opened. A robot slid up to Gladias, carrying his tea and rice and vegetable dish. Gladias picked up both with his hands. He thanked the robot, and the robot slid back out of the room.

"Do you want to go upstairs and check out the roof?", Verdow asked.

"Sure", Zei answered.

Gladias, Seila and Zei stood up. Verdow walked out of the room and began to walk through the corridor. The three of them followed, Gladias still holding his tea in one hand and his food in the other.

Verdow led them up a staircase, and reached a door which opened automatically. They stepped out.

To their left, they could see the main commercial district of Meldan. There were buildings of various styles, some that were aesthetic imitations of something older and almost medieval, and others that were openly modern and futuristic. The building that looked like an aeroplane stood out from among the others, slightly spoiling the view. The trees are only good at covering it up when you're at ground level yourself, Gladias thought.

Further left of the commercial district, they could see the grey and purple Greater Plum Harbor. The whole thing was a square nearly a kilometer wide, and they could see many of its buildings clearly from where they were. And on the right edge of the commercial district, Gladias could make out the large concert venue.

In front of them, they could see the Kalimar district. From where they stood, it looked not too different from a forest. Tall trees covered up most of the area, with only a few buildings poking up just barely above them. After scanning the area quickly, Gladias spotted the headquarters of Silverchat.

To their right, they could see the mountain covered with trees. They were already partway up the mountain, about forty meters higher than most of the rest of Meldan. But about two hundred meters to their right, the mountain began sloping upward properly. Only about half of the apartment buildings shaped like oversided medieval-style castle towers were visible from where they were. The mountain looked much larger and more imposing from close up, Gladias thought.

"Probably not as beautiful as the views in Northglade?", Verdow asked.

"I like the green here. I don't think I could handle being up north and dealing with several months of no green and only snow."

"And besides, Meldan is my home."
